text:
===== FILE 12627__1.pdf =====
I submit this comment in strong, unequivocal opposition to the Department of Veterans Affairs’ 
(VA) proposed rule that would end or severely restrict abortion care for veterans and their 
dependents, including in cases of rape, incest, or where the health of the pregnant person is at 
risk. As a pro-abortion, anti-Trump American, I object to this proposal on medical, ethical, legal, 
operational, and moral grounds. This rule would harm veterans, undermine evidence-based 
medicine, and betray the VA’s duty of care. 
 
Veterans deserve comprehensive, evidence-based health care, not political interference. 
 
The VA’s mission is to provide medically necessary care to those who served. In 2022, after the 
Supreme Court ended federal constitutional protection for abortion, VA implemented a narrow, 
clinically grounded policy to offer abortion in cases of rape or incest and when a clinician 
determines the life or health of the veteran is endangered. That policy aligned the VA with basic 
standards of medical necessity and protected the most vulnerable veterans.  
 
The proposed ban reverses those limited protections and would yank essential care from 
veterans and their families, even in profound medical emergencies or after sexual violence. 
Reporting indicates the change would eliminate most abortions currently allowed at VA facilities, 
rolling care back to pre-2022 exclusions and, in some descriptions, even limiting coverage to 
only imminent life-threatening scenarios, effectively abandoning health-preserving care and 
cases of rape or incest. That is not medical decision-making; it is political punishment. 
 
The medical record is clear: denying abortion care worsens health outcomes. 
 
Major longitudinal research (i.e. the Turnaway Study) found that people denied wanted 
abortions face significantly worse health outcomes, including higher rates of life-threatening 
complications such as eclampsia and infection, greater chronic pain, and worse long-term 
physical and mental health compared to those who received care. These harms extend to 
families and children through increased economic insecurity and reduced well-being.  
 
The United States already has unacceptably high maternal mortality compared with peer 
nations. Even as rates fluctuated after the pandemic spike, recent CDC data show persistent, 
stark racial disparities and ongoing risk: for example, in 2023 the maternal mortality rate for 
Black women (50.3 per 100,000) remained far higher than for White, Hispanic, or Asian women. 
Denying timely abortion care (particularly care that preserves a patient’s health) pushes patients 
deeper into this danger. 
 
Pregnancy itself can be medically risky; obstetric emergencies (hemorrhage, hypertensive 
crises, cardiomyopathy, sepsis) demand rapid, clinician-directed options. Eliminating abortion as 
a tool to preserve a patient’s health forces clinicians into unacceptable delays or into transferring 
patients, compounding risk. The national context (maternity care deserts and system strain) 
means veterans will be harmed by any policy that strips options from their doctors. 
Women veterans (and many other veterans) already face access 
barriers the VA is designed to fix 

 
Women veterans (one of the fastest-growing veteran populations) experience unique, 
well-documented access gaps in reproductive health. RAND testimony and congressional 
research on VA policy underscore that abortion can be medically necessary and that the VA’s 
2022 action removed harmful exclusions (including on abortion counseling) to ensure veterans 
could get clinically indicated care in narrow, critical circumstances. Re-imposing a categorical 
ban ignores that record and sets the VA against evidence-based practice. 
 
The burden will not be equal. Veterans living in rural areas, low-income veterans, veterans of 
color, 2SLGBTQIA+ veterans, and survivors of military sexual trauma will face the steepest 
barriers if the VA refuses care. For those who cannot safely travel or pay out-of-pocket, a ban 
does not end abortion. It ends access to safe abortion, pushing people toward later, riskier care 
or forcing them to carry dangerous or traumatic pregnancies. The evidence shows that is 
harmful, avoidable, and wrong. 
 
The proposed ban is arbitrary and capricious: it disregards evidence, reliance interests, and 
clinical judgment 
 
Under basic administrative law principles, an agency must consider relevant evidence, reliance 
interests, and the consequences of policy reversal. In 2022, the VA explicitly recognized that 
abortions needed to preserve life or health and in cases of rape or incest fall within medical 
necessity. Veterans and clinicians have relied on that life- and health-preserving framework for 
years. Ripping it away without a robust, evidence-based explanation, especially in the face of 
national data on maternal risk and the Turnaway Study’s clear findings, would be arbitrary and 
capricious. 
 
A categorical ban also substitutes political preference for individualized medical judgment. The 
2022 policy required case-by-case determinations by VA clinicians in consultation with their 
patients, and, crucially, accepted a veteran’s self-report of rape or incest as sufficient, protecting 
survivors from retraumatizing hurdles. Returning to a blanket prohibition would silence clinical 
expertise and endanger veterans whose health is at risk but who do not meet a narrow, 
after-the-fact definition of “imminent” life endangerment. 
 
Operationally, the ban will increase costs, delays, and risk for the VA 
system: 
 
Forcing veterans to seek care outside the VA for a time-sensitive medical service increases 
delays, logistical failure points, and downstream costs (including emergency care for 
preventable complications, high-risk deliveries, NICU stays, and long-term disability). It will 
strain coordination across jurisdictions with conflicting laws, complicate referrals, and increase 
clinician moral distress and attrition. Those are foreseeable, avoidable operational harms. 
Evidence across the health system shows that earlier, clinician-directed abortion care reduces 
severe morbidity, whereas denial increases emergency interventions and complications.  ￼ ￼ 
 

Ethically, this rule betrays the people who served. 
 
Veterans put on the uniform believing they were defending freedom. Telling those same people, 
many of whom have survived trauma, that the government will force them to remain pregnant 
after rape or to continue a pregnancy that threatens their health is the opposite of freedom. It is 
coercion, and it is cruelty. 
 
This is not an abstract debate. With bans advancing elsewhere, courts are already entertaining 
federal actions that curtail access and funding, creating chaos that lands on patients. The VA 
should be a bulwark against chaos, not a participant in it. 
 
What the VA should do instead 
​
1. Withdraw the proposed rule and retain the 2022 framework that permits abortion when 
needed to preserve a veteran’s life or health and in cases of rape or incest. That policy is 
narrow, clinically grounded, and humane.  
2. Affirm clinician judgment and case-by-case decision-making rather than imposing categorical 
bans. 
3. Publish a robust evidence review of maternal morbidity and mortality, with attention to the 
Turnaway Study and CDC data, and explain how VA policy will reduce, not increase, 
preventable harm. 
4. Protect survivors of sexual violence by maintaining self-report standards and trauma-informed 
access pathways. 
5. Invest in continuity of reproductive care, including counseling, contraception, miscarriage 
management, and abortion where medically indicated to reduce emergency utilization and 
adverse outcomes. 
 
The Bottom Line 
 
Abortion is health care. Veterans and their families deserve the full spectrum of evidence-based 
care, free from political interference. The proposed ban would endanger patients, contravene 
medical evidence, and betray the VA’s duty to those who served. For all of these 
reasons—medical, legal, operational, ethical—I urge the Department to withdraw this rule 
immediately and to preserve (at minimum) the 2022 protections for cases of rape, incest, and 
threats to a patient’s life or health. Anything less would be an abdication of the VA’s commitment 
to care. 
 
I submit this of my own accord, 
 
Brooklyn Wagner
